the free energies of folding of the mutant proteins are more sensitive to the changes in the hydrophobicity of their side chains than to changes in their size.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of amino-acid replacements are not always consistent, and therefore, it is not possible to draw generalizations from the data.
the effects of point mutations on protein folding are complex.
the folding mechanism of a protein is determined by its primary structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the folding of a globular protein can be described by a series of discrete steps, each of which is characterized by a specific free energy of activation.

the folding of a small globular protein is a complex process, and the folding of a protein can be altered by a single amino acid replacement, even though the change in the free energy for folding may be small.
the effects of mutations are not only determined by the properties of amino acid residues but also by the properties of the environment in which they are placed.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the folding and stability of a given protein are determined not by the properties of the individual amino acids that constitute the polypeptide chain but by the properties of specific amino acid side chains in the native state.
the effect of a given amino acid replacement depends on the nature of the protein, the location of the replacement, and the conditions under which folding occurs.
the folding of a protein involves a complex interplay between the native structure and the folding intermediates.
